<thoughtml>
  <evaluation name="Tutoring trial">
    <findings>
      <finding outcome="overall achievement" result="positive">
        Participating students improved more than students in the comparison class.
      </finding>
      <finding outcome="homework completion" result="positive" evidence="teacher observations">
        Teachers observed better homework completion among tutoring participants.
      </finding>
      <finding outcome="attendance" result="small improvement">
        Attendance gains were limited.
      </finding>
    </findings>

    <limitations>
      <limitation type="selection bias">
        Participation was voluntary, and tutoring families were more motivated at baseline.
      </limitation>
      <limitation type="confounding">
        The greater improvement may partly reflect pre-existing motivation rather than tutoring.
      </limitation>
      <limitation type="measurement">
        Homework completion evidence was based on teacher observations and may be subject to observer bias.
      </limitation>
      <limitation type="generalizability">
        Results from this trial may not apply equally to students or families who would not volunteer.
      </limitation>
    </limitations>

    <causal_hypothesis>
      Tutoring may improve achievement by providing additional instruction, support, and accountability, which may also encourage students to complete homework. However, motivated families may independently produce better engagement and outcomes, so the tutoring effect cannot be isolated confidently from the available comparison.
    </causal_hypothesis>

    <confidence>
      <outcome name="achievement" level="moderate-low">
        The observed advantage is encouraging, but voluntary participation substantially weakens causal confidence.
      </outcome>
      <outcome name="homework completion" level="low-moderate">
        The pattern is consistent with a tutoring benefit, but the evidence is observational.
      </outcome>
      <outcome name="attendance" level="low">
        Gains were small and do not provide strong evidence of an attendance effect.
      </outcome>
      <adoption level="cautious">
        Adopt or extend the program as a monitored pilot rather than as a proven school-wide intervention. Use randomized or matched assignment where feasible, measure baseline motivation, and track achievement, homework, and attendance for participating and nonparticipating students.
      </adoption>
    </confidence>
  </evaluation>
</thoughtml>
